an1.258:1.1: This must be the Sujātā who, according to legend, offered the meal to the Buddha immediately before awakening near “the town of Senā” in Uruvelā. She does not seem to be mentioned elsewhere in the early texts; there are several Sujātās, but they are different people. The commentary says she was the daughter of the town landowner named “Senānī”. However, this requires the spelling _senānīnigama_ (or _senānīgāma_), whereas the spelling in the early texts is _senā-nigama_, “the town of Senā”. Buddhaghosa explains the word both ways: the “military town” (_senānigama_, due to the longstanding military garrison there), or the “town belonging to Senānī” (_senānīnigama_). Given that the latter spelling is not supported by early texts, nor is there substantive evidence that Senānī even existed, I take it as the “military town”. Her second name is spelled either _seniyadhītā_ or _senānidhītā_. I accept the former, where _seniya_ means “military” and the suffix _-dhītā_ is pleonastic (cf. _sakyaputta_ = “Sakyan”, etc.), the whole meaning “woman from the military (town)”.
an1.259:1.1: Visākhā was a wealthy lady of Sāvatthī who appears frequently, especially in the Aṅguttara, Udāna, and Vinaya, as a dedicated donor and practitioner (eg. [an3.70](), [an8.43](), [an8.47](), [an8.49]()). She is named for the 16th lunar asterism (Libra) in the Artharva Veda system, under which she was presumably born. The commentaries say her eldest son was named Migāra, although in their elaborate backstory they also say she is named for her father-in-law Migāra, who named her his mother as a title of honor after she introduced him to the Dhamma. She built a large stilt longhouse as residence for the Saṅgha, which was named after her [pli-tv-kd16:14.1.1]().
an1.260:1.1: While Khujjuttarā is noted as a leading laywoman several times in the Suttas (eg. [sn17.24:1.4](), we find no further details. For that we turn again to the commentaries, which say she was a serving lady in the court of Queen Sāmāvatī of Kosambī. She was assiduous in learning the Dhamma, and the Itivuttaka as a whole is said to have been memorized by her and taught to the ladies of the court.
an1.261:1.1: The tragic death of Queen Sāmāvatī and 500 ladies of her court in a fire at Kosambī is related at [ud7.10](). King Udena was away and hence escaped. No explanation for her power of love (_mettā_) is found in the early texts. The commentaries weave an elaborate tale of a jealous co-wife, who after a long campaign of abuse and manipulation, persuaded the king to execute Sāmāvatī. Due to her love, however, the arrow turned aside.
an1.262:1.1: Uttarā, Nanda’s mother is probably the same person as Veḷukaṇṭakī, Nanda’s mother, so her full style would have been “Uttarā of Veḷukaṇṭaka, mother of Nanda”. She lived in the distant Southern Hills, where she rose early to recite the verses of “The Way to the Far Shore”, then presented a meal offering to the Saṅgha ([an7.53]()). While conversing with Sāriputta, she attested to her skill in absorption. Her offering was noted and praised by the Buddha ([an6.37]()). She was said to be a standard for laywomen at [an2.133]() and [an4.176:4.2]().
an1.263:1.1: Suppavāsā’s generosity is recognized in [ud4.57](), but she is better known for the unusual circumstances of her pregnancy as related in [ud2.8]().
an1.264:1.1: Suppiyā, who lived with her husband in Varanasi, offered medicine to sick monks. One required meat broth, but no meat was available in the city, so she had broth made with flesh from her own thigh. As a result, the Buddha banned human flesh, and required that monks check before eating meat ([pli-tv-kd6:23.1.1](); see also [mn55:5.2]()).
an1.265:1.1: Kātiyānī is not mentioned elsewhere in early texts. The commentaries say she was friends with Kāḷī in Kuraraghara in Avanti, where they realized the Dhamma through the teaching of Soṇa of the Sharp Ears.
an1.266:1.1: See the note on Nakula’s father ([an1.257]()).
an1.267:1.1: At [an10.26](), Kāḷī questions Mahākaccāna in Avanti on the text of “The Maidens’ Questions”. | It seems likely that the Pali canon was transmitted to Sri Lanka from Avanti by Mahinda, who studied there in the school originally established by Mahākaccāna. The prominent roles ascribed to Kāḷī and Kātiyānī here, as students of Soṇa and Mahākaccāna, and the connection of Mahākaccāna, Soṇa, and Kāḷī with textual transmission, suggest they were included in this list to celebrate the local heroes renowned for establishing Buddhism in Avanti, whose school gave shape to the Pali canon as we have it today.
